title: A year on the porch
hookLine: a year with Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus

lines: WHERE CAN I FIND MEN LIKE THAT?
cards: A merchant from Cyprus named Zeno has been shipwrecked and lost his cargo. Stranded in Athens, he wanders into a bookshop and hears someone reading about Socrates. He asks the bookseller: where can I find men like that?
The story goes that a philosopher happened to walk past right then, and the bookseller pointed. Years later, Zeno began teaching in a public colonnade on the edge of the marketplace.
That covered walkway gave the school its name, and gave this whole year its name too.

teach.b: First, the porch itself. In Greek, stoa poikilē: the painted porch, a long roofed walkway whose walls carried well-known paintings, including the battle of Marathon. Anyone could walk in.

Zeno taught there, in public, and his followers were called the people of the stoa: Stoics. A philosophy named not after a founder but after a public place where anyone could stand and listen. Second, the road.
It started on day three hundred thirty-two with a little handbook, Epictetus's teaching boiled down by his student Arrian, meant to be kept at hand.
Then the longer Discourses, Epictetus arguing and joking with his students. Then Seneca, letter by letter, essay by essay. Then all twelve books of Marcus, straight through.
And lately, the wider porch: the founders before, the neighbors next door, the people who came after, the turning year, and the porch in ordinary life. Third, four very different voices.
A merchant who lost everything at sea. A man once enslaved, who limped. A rich adviser at a dangerous court.
An emperor writing to himself on campaign. They didn't agree on everything, and they weren't saints.

teach.h: FOUR VOICES, THE SAME PLAIN QUESTIONS.
teach.b: But each kept asking the same plain questions: what is up to me? What is good? How should I live with other people?

teach.h: A YEAR OF DAYS, WOVEN IN.
teach.b: Fourth, what a year does. One lesson is a thought.
A year of them is a road, with your own days woven through it.

how: Some people finishing a year of Stoic reading reread their earliest notes and ask how the practice has changed them, if at all.

games.q: you're Zeno, shipwrecked in Athens, and you've just heard about Socrates in a bookshop. what do you ask?
o: where can I find men like that?
games.why: the story goes that a philosopher walked by just then, and the bookseller pointed: follow him.

practice: Go back, in your mind or your notes, to day three hundred thirty-two, the handbook for the road, whose line was keep it at hand: what were you carrying then, and what's changed, even slightly?
Maybe nothing obvious; that's honest too. Then let the year's voices pass by, Zeno, Epictetus, Seneca, Marcus, and notice which one, if any, you'd most like to sit beside.

wordCard.voice: Stoa poikilē, the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught in public, open to anyone who walked in off the street. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the painted porch in Athens, where Zeno taught.

carryVoice: Your line: what is up to me. Four voices, one plain question, a whole year long. Day six hundred eighty-nine counts.
